## Seven Security Domains

Several rigorously audited challenges spanning the offensive, defensive, and investigative cybersecurity landscape.

### Web

Modern web security flaws: authentication bypass, server-side request forgery, injection primitives, and API logic vulnerabilities.

### Crypto

Mathematical cryptanalysis: lattice reductions, weak RSA key generation, custom stream ciphers, and elliptic curve edge cases.

### Pwn

Binary exploitation: memory corruption, stack overflows, format string vulnerabilities, custom shellcode, and ROP chain fabrication.

### Forensics

Digital incident reconstruction: volatile memory dumps (Volatility), deep packet captures, raw disk images, and covert steganography.

### Misc

Automation and algorithmic challenges: dynamic socket scripting, esoteric encodings, hardware logic analysis, and unconventional puzzles.

### Rev

Reverse engineering: disassembly, decompilation (Ghidra/IDA), binary unpackers, anti-debugging mechanisms, and custom bytecode interpreters.

# How the robot works

Twenty-one days, two robot generations and a team of Claude models, built to play a 31 day security CTF against the clock. This is the whole machine: how it is put together, where the AI sits, how I knew what was true, and every morning it went wrong.

By Wizdumb

Every morning at 09:00 ET a new set of challenges dropped: file forensics, malicious script analysis, binary reverse engineering, Android, and from Day 19, live web exploitation. I built a robot to play them. Known shapes run as plain deterministic code, with no model anywhere in the path. An unknown shape opens a gap loop where Claude agents write a patch, a sandboxed judge checks it against everything the robot has ever been graded on, and the running lane picks it up without a restart.

4thoverall: one of 56 teams that completed every check, on 1,885 points, and 0.44 s off the podium

72.5 sbest morning (Day 29): release to the last of 21 checks, all CORRECT. Next team 153.8 s.

Task
    An APK whose manifest and code tell a story about a real Android weakness. The answer is an `ANS-` plus 16-hex code behind a named codec in a bundled JSON asset.
Example
    

codec: xor, key 29, data: base64 produces ANS-…

Technique
    Treat the story as a decoy and undo the codec. The `ANS-` pattern is a correctness check for a depth-two search over the codec registry, followed by six bounded brute-force families.
Escalation
    From Day 23 the code had to be computed: a static dex bytecode interpreter, then a static x86-64 stepper for a native library, reflection, and split APKs.

Exported components, deep links, intent injection, backups, providers, WebView bridges, cleartext, trust-all TLS, keystore misuse, JNI, encrypted strings, reflection, emulator checks, integrity signals, split APKs, a white-box table codec, and a rolling XOR.

### Web live targets, Day 19 on

Task
    A live site built on demand. Exploit the bug and submit a `proof_` token. Mastery gives several targets at once, and a target dies a few minutes after start.
Technique
    Detect the technique by probing the page, not by trusting the challenge name. A toolkit covers fetch, forms, cookies, JWT, Flask sessions, access logs and packet captures. Requests outside the named host are refused in code.
Curveball
    Day 31: the header the app read its role from was named only in a `Vary` response header, and every tool read response bodies, never headers. It cost about 228 s and, by four-tenths of a second, the podium.

Backup exposure, IDOR, SQL injection, LFI, XSS, session fixation, CSRF, upload, template families, second-order injection, over-posting, command injection, reset flows, GraphQL, webhook trust, XXE, deserialisation, access-control bypasses, host poisoning, NoSQL, websockets, forwarded headers, delegated identity, job queues, and proxy trust.

Across lanes, surprises fell into six types: answer wording for a known fact, a new question on a known format, a new Mastery shape or layer, a new file format, a new language or technique, and infrastructure faults. Wording problems hit the first day of a fact. New capability hit metadata and script almost daily. Shape problems hit Mastery first, because Mastery combines shapes the Time Trial does not show.

# CTF: 2026 Huntress

Crashnburn

11 min read

·

1 day ago

--

Listen

Share

The Huntress CTF was a month-long experience. It had over 1,600 participants throughout the month, and this is my non-technical write up of how I finished second. The goal was to document the ups and downs I felt with this style of CTF because it was a unique experience. Check out my github for more details.

The CTF went like this:

Each day 3 new problems come out per lane. The problems are “Single Solve” which serves as your learning problem, “Timed Trial” which gives you a variant and a time limit, and “Mastery Mode” which puts everything on steroids and gives you multiple variants. Each day there were also multiple lanes (metadata forensics, script analysis, mobile, binary, etc). There was no dynamic scoring so the final day is what mattered if you were all caught up.

## Starting Out

I started the 2026 Huntress CTF a couple of days after it started, so I had most of the month to understand the problems and fine tune my solvers. 
## The Fall

During a month-long CTF, you get the full rollercoaster of emotions. I started slow, ramped up, and eventually settled into a pretty good rhythm. Then everything started falling apart.

The days became unpredictable. Each day involved a different lane spazzing out. Some days were worse than others.

On Day 22 the binary lane needed three rounds of fixes, and a Time Trial config came back as “none” when my solver expected a value.

Day 23 was the worst. The script lane got stuck installing, failing and retrying the same answer for about 40 minutes… what is happening.

On Day 24 the metadata Mastery bundle lost 12 minutes because my tooling didn’t know what to do with an “accepted, N remaining” response.

On Day 25 the mobile lane took 24 minutes to untangle Dalvik wide-register arguments because it forgot that a 64-bit argument uses two registers… I didn’t know this either but apparently Claude thought we should both spend 24 minutes finding out.

Every day, I would analyze the issues and attempt to fix them, but I was really just applying band aids to a broken system. I am examining the new lane, it is a reverse engineering problem, SHA1-hulud.

Anti-emulation tricks galore. Progress is made, roadblocks are hit, I argue with Claude, I do some research, I spin up a windows VM to help out, I need a break, and finally the beast is slain. We are in 26th place.

I was now worried what this meant for the last day though, so I checked the discord and found out that the last day would be back to normal. I wrap up my fixes for the day, run regression tests to make sure I didn’t break anything, think about making bigger changes, but decided to go to sleep.

The final day happens and things went about as well as they could. There was a silly mistake with web that cost a lot of time, but I was able to finish in 2nd place.

## Conclusion

This was an amazing event. It is the first CTF I have done in a few years, and it was great to go in and use AI to the max for this. I was initially hesitant about doing the whole thing but I am glad I did.

Personally, I took a long time to mind shift into this style of CTF. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
